result:
The way we experience time is a curious thing. When I was a child, summer holidays felt like a vast, sun-drenched continent to explore. A single afternoon could hold the entirety of a world built from cardboard and imagination. Now, weeks sometimes blur into one another, marked only by the accumulation of tasks on a list.

It’s as though our perception is tied to novelty. For a child, almost everything is new—a first bike ride, a firefly in a jar, the taste of a strange fruit. Each new sensation stretches the moment, carving it into memory. With familiarity, the brain’s recording slows. The commute, the routine, the well-worn path—they become a low hum in the background.

But I believe this can be countered, not by seeking constant novelty, but by cultivating presence. There is a profound difference between drinking a cup of coffee and simply consuming caffeine. To notice the weight of the ceramic mug, the curl of steam, the bitterness on the tongue—that is to pause the relentless forward march for just an instant.

Maybe time isn’t a line we travel, but a texture we feel. In moments of flow, whether creating something or truly listening to another person, hours dissolve into minutes. In moments of anticipation or dread, minutes expand into hours. Our inner clock is a poet, not a physicist, measuring life in quality, not just quantity. The challenge, then, is to be present enough to let the meaningful moments breathe.
